pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–8 years

- **Topic:** How Plant Parts Work

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS2 Y3 Plants):** "identify and describe the functions of different parts of flowering plants: roots, stem/trunk, leaves and flowers." Non-statutory guidance stresses the structure–function relationship — 'every part has a job to do': roots and stem for nutrition and support, leaves for nutrition, flowers for reproduction.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 4-LS1-1, nearest anchor):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-LS1-1]." The US frame is the same structure–function idea, pushed toward argument-from-evidence.

- **Operational details:** This is the function partner to Parts of a Plant: children already name the parts, now they learn what each DOES — roots absorb water and minerals and anchor the plant, stem transports water up and holds the plant up to the light, leaves make food using sunlight, flowers make seeds for reproduction. Teach function through evidence, not assertion: the classic celery/white-flower-in-coloured-water investigation makes stem transport VISIBLE, and covering a leaf or removing roots shows what fails. Emphasise 'every part has a job'. Keep 'leaves make food' at the level of 'using sunlight' — the photosynthesis equation is KS3. This underpins water transport, pollination/seed formation, and structures-for-survival.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A→B (concrete moving to early-explanatory, ≈7–8, KS2 Y3). Children can state the function of roots, stem, leaves and flowers and support at least the stem-transport claim with observation. Appropriate: functions evidenced by simple investigations. NOT appropriate yet: xylem/phloem naming, photosynthesis chemistry, mineral-ion detail. Watch the deep 'plants get their food from the soil' misconception — here is where 'leaves make the food, roots only take in water and minerals' must be taught explicitly.
bestPractices: Teach each part's function through evidence, not assertion — e.g. coloured-water uptake to show stem transport, covering a leaf or removing roots to show what fails.
Explicitly separate 'roots take in water and minerals' from 'leaves make the food', directly confronting the plants-eat-soil misconception.
Use the structure–function framing 'every part has a job to do', linking back to the named parts from the prior topic.
Keep leaf food-making at 'using sunlight' level; reserve the photosynthesis equation and xylem/phloem for KS3.
Push toward simple argument-from-evidence (NGSS 4-LS1-1): ask children to justify a part's job from what they observed.
keyRepresentations: Coloured-water / celery / white-flower dye-uptake investigation showing stem transport.
A part→function table (roots: absorb & anchor; stem: transport & support; leaves: make food; flowers: reproduce).
Deprivation demonstrations (leaf covered from light; roots removed) linking part to consequence.
Labelled plant diagram annotated with each part's job.
commonMisconceptions: 'Plants get their food from the soil / through their roots' — not recognising leaves make the food using sunlight.
Thinking the stem is only for support, missing its transport role (or vice versa).
Believing roots 'suck up food' rather than water and minerals.
Seeing flowers as decorative rather than the plant's reproductive organs.

learn.summary: For ages 7–8, teach the functions of flowering-plant parts (roots, stem, leaves, flowers) through evidence rather than assertion — the recommended teaching approach for this topic, with DfE KS2 Y3 explicitly supporting investigation of how water is transported in plants. Children should move from naming parts to explaining what each DOES: roots absorb water and minerals and anchor the plant; the stem transports water upward and holds the plant up to the light; leaves make food using sunlight; flowers make seeds for reproduction. The central recommended teaching move is test-and-consequence — disable or deprive a part and observe what fails — with the classic coloured-water/celery investigation making stem transport visibly real. The highest-priority conceptual target is confronting the 'plants eat soil' misconception by explicitly separating 'roots take in water and minerals' from 'leaves make the food using sunlight'. Keep food-making at the 'using sunlight' level; the photosynthesis equation and xylem/phloem naming are beyond this stage.

activities.title: Plant test-lab: switch each part on or off and watch what happens
feedback: If the learner says roots or soil provide the plant's food: the covered-leaf test shows the plant kept from light weakens even with plenty of water and soil, while the lit plant stays healthy — so the soil is not giving ready-made food; the leaves make food using light, while roots take up water and minerals.
If the learner thinks the stem is only for support: the dye climbing up the stem into the leaves shows the stem is also the plant's plumbing, carrying water from roots to leaves.
If the learner can't connect the dark cover to starving: point to where sunlight normally lands — the leaves. Blocking light stops food-making, which is why the plant weakens despite having water.

Reinforce: each test gives evidence for one main job (roots take in water, the stem carries water, leaves make food using light); anchoring, support and the flower's job of making seeds need other evidence, such as gently tugging a rooted plant or watching seeds form as a flower fades.
activities.rationale: Function can be made observable through test-and-consequence: making a part fail and observing the outcome turns each 'job' into evidenced cause-and-effect. This evidence-first stance is the recommended teaching approach for this topic rather than a proven-superior method, and DfE KS2 Y3 explicitly supports investigating how water is transported in plants, which underwrites the dye-uptake test. The visible dye-uptake and leaf-covering tests are intended to directly target the dominant misconception that plants get ready-made food from the soil.
sourceClaims: DfE KS2 Y3 also covers investigating how water is transported within plants (the basis for a visible dye-uptake investigation to evidence stem function).
The belief that plants obtain their food from the soil (rather than making it in the leaves) is a persistent misconception that this topic must directly confront.

DfE KS2 Year 3 statutory content requires pupils to 'identify and describe the functions of different parts of flowering plants: roots, stem/trunk, leaves and flowers'; guidance frames this as structure–function ('every part has a job'): roots/stem for nutrition and support, leaves for nutrition, flowers for reproduction.
learnerActions: Start with a healthy plant and predict what each part does before testing it.

In the on-screen model, remove or disable the roots and observe the result (the model plant droops because it can no longer take in water); restore them and watch it recover. A real plant pulled up and left without water wilts, and its roots cannot simply be put back.
Stand the plant in blue-dyed water and watch the colour travel up the stem and spread into the leaf veins and petals — evidence that the stem carries water from roots to leaves.

Cover the leaves from the light while the plant still has water, and compare it with an identical, equally watered plant left in the light: over time (days to weeks for a real plant) the covered plant becomes pale and weak while the lit plant stays healthy — evidence that the leaves need sunlight to make the plant's food, and that the roots are not pulling ready-made food from the soil.

After each test, state which job it gave evidence for: absorbing water (roots), carrying water (stem), making food using light (leaves). Notice that none of these tests shows anchoring, support or the flower's job of making seeds; talk about those jobs separately, using other evidence.
Pair the dye test with the real celery-in-food-colouring (or white flower in coloured water) classroom investigation as a hands-on complement.
activities.intendedInsight: Each plant part has a specific job, and you can gather evidence for it by seeing what fails when the part is removed, deprived, or blocked — function becomes an observed cause-and-effect rather than a stated fact.

activities.title: Tap-each-part diagram: the job behind every structure
feedback: If the learner matches a part to the wrong job, replay the animation and ask them to describe what the part is doing and what the plant needs it for.
Prompt: 'Which part makes the food?' If they answer roots, highlight the leaf animation and the role of sunlight.
activities.rationale: A reveal-the-job diagram maps structure to function and connects to prior part-naming. It presents the functions directly, so it is suited to delivery and consolidation alongside the evidence-building lab rather than as the sole route to the concept.
sourceClaims: DfE KS2 Year 3 statutory content requires pupils to 'identify and describe the functions of different parts of flowering plants: roots, stem/trunk, leaves and flowers'; guidance frames this as structure–function ('every part has a job'): roots/stem for nutrition and support, leaves for nutrition, flowers for reproduction.
learnerActions: Tap each part of a labelled plant diagram to reveal a short animation of its job: roots drawing in water, water rising in the stem, sunlight hitting the leaf to make food, the flower forming seeds.
Read or say the one-line function for each part as it is revealed.
Link each part back to its name from earlier work on naming plant parts, then annotate a labelled diagram with each part's job in your own words.
activities.intendedInsight: Every named part of the plant maps to a specific function — structure and function go together.

activities.title: Match and check: part to job
feedback: Correct answer to 'which part makes food?' is the leaves (using sunlight); roots take in water and minerals from the soil but do not make the food.
If a learner selects 'roots make food', restate: roots take up water and minerals, but food is MADE in the leaves using light.
If a learner says the flower is just for decoration or to look nice: the flower's job is to make seeds so the plant can grow new plants — this links forward to later work on pollination and seeds.
activities.rationale: Direct matching and targeted questions check the structure–function mapping and surface the 'roots make food' and 'flowers are decorative' misconceptions. This checks recognition and recall, so it should follow — not replace — the evidence-building investigation.
sourceClaims: The belief that plants obtain their food from the soil (rather than making it in the leaves) is a persistent misconception that this topic must directly confront.
learnerActions: Match each part to its job: roots → absorb water and minerals and anchor; stem → transport water and support; leaves → make food using sunlight; flowers → make seeds.
Answer targeted questions such as 'Which part makes the plant's food?' and 'What do the roots take in?', deliberately rejecting the option that says roots make or suck up food.
Explain the reason for each match, not just the pairing.
activities.intendedInsight: Confirm the structure–function mapping and explicitly reject the idea that roots or soil supply ready-made food.

activities.title: Convince the plant scientist: argue from what you observed
feedback: Strong answers point to specific observations (the dark-covered plant weakened compared with the plant in light, despite having water; the dye rose up the stem) rather than restating facts.
If the learner only asserts the job without evidence, prompt: 'What did you SEE that shows this?'
activities.rationale: NGSS 4-LS1-1 points toward argument from evidence. An in-role exchange exercises justification and reasoning, which suits consolidation after the functions have been established by observation.
sourceClaims: NGSS 4-LS1-1 asks pupils to [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-LS1-1] — the structure–function anchor for plant part functions.
learnerActions: Respond in role to a 'plant scientist' who asks you to justify each part's job: 'Convince me the leaves, not the roots, make the plant's food — what's your evidence?'
Cite what you saw in the investigations (the covered plant weakening compared with the plant in the light, the dye climbing the stem) as the reason for each claim.
Answer follow-up challenges, e.g. explain why a plant kept in a dark box could not make food even with plenty of water and soil.
activities.intendedInsight: A part's job can be justified from observed evidence — building toward constructing an argument from evidence.

constraints: Keep leaf food-making at the 'using sunlight' level; the photosynthesis equation, xylem/phloem naming, and mineral-ion detail are for a later stage (KS3) and should not be introduced here.
The top priority is explicitly separating 'roots take in water and minerals' from 'leaves make the food', directly confronting the persistent 'plants get food from the soil' misconception.

Reveal-the-job diagrams and matching tasks present or check functions but do not require the learner to build the evidence themselves; use them to deliver and consolidate, not as the sole route to the concept.

Matching and multiple-choice questions can check recognition and recall but do not by themselves elicit independent reasoning; the argument-from-evidence task is where the learner constructs justification.
A screen simulation of removing or depriving parts is a model; pair it with the real celery/white-flower-in-coloured-water investigation so children see the effect in a living plant.
Physical paper/card diagrams and on-screen models offer different experiences; neither is uniquely required, and the dialogue, diagram, and lab each serve distinct purposes.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the four cited sources were marked unverified in the original row (NGSS 4-LS1-1 and the Rueschhoff plant-misconceptions reference); their claims are retained as supplied but not independently confirmed here.

The phrase 'teach function through evidence, not assertion' comes from the agent's operational notes in the source row, not a verbatim curriculum quotation; summary and rationale wording was corrected to attribute it as the recommended teaching approach rather than DfE guidance, while DfE's genuine support for investigating water transport is cited for the dye evidence.

The original description and evidence fields state the stem transports 'food around the plant', while the main teaching emphasis (and KS2 Y3) centres water transport up the stem; food transport (phloem/translocation) is real but beyond this stage and has been kept out of learner-facing actions to avoid overreaching. Reviewer may wish to reconcile the description/evidence wording.

The stated timing in the original ('within seconds the plant droops', dye 'crawls visibly up the stem') is an animation convenience; real plants respond over longer timescales — framed as a model so learners are not misled about real-world speed.
The original artefact-selection rationale asserted test-and-consequence is 'best'; this was softened to qualified wording since no source establishes comparative efficacy.

probeDeeper: The roots take up water — so is water the same as food? What's the difference?
If a plant had plenty of water and soil but was kept in a dark box, could it still make food? Why not?
What is the flower's job — what does it make?
Why does the stem matter — what would happen if water couldn't travel up it?
assess.correctAnswer: The LEAVES make the plant's food, using sunlight (plus water from the roots and air). The plant does NOT take ready-made food from the soil — the roots take up water and minerals, but the food itself is made in the leaves. Full marks put food-MAKING in the leaves and reject 'food comes from the soil'.

errorPatterns.pattern: plants get their food ready-made from the soil ('the roots suck up food')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate 'food' from 'water and minerals': roots take up water + a little mineral, but the leaves MAKE the food using light. Preview the air-and-water evidence.
errorPatterns.distractor: The roots suck up food from the soil to feed the plant.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: names roots (or soil) as the food source rather than the leaves making food

errorPatterns.pattern: leaves are for breathing/decoration, not food-making
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point to where light lands — the leaves. That's the food factory. A plant kept dark can't make food even with water.
errorPatterns.distractor: The leaves are just there to look nice or to breathe.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: assigns the food job to roots or 'the whole plant', not the leaves

errorPatterns.pattern: the flower's job is to be pretty, not reproduction
errorPatterns.nextMove: Flowers are for making seeds — the plant's way of making new plants. Link to the coming pollination work.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: can't say the flower makes seeds/new plants

responseLevels.gap: Says the roots/soil feed the plant; can't locate food-making in the leaves.
responseLevels.full: Locates food-making in the leaves (using light), casts roots as water/mineral uptake (not food), names the flower's reproductive job, and rejects 'food from soil' — explaining why a dark-kept plant starves despite water.
responseLevels.partial: Says leaves make food but still also credits the soil as a food source, or matches parts to jobs mechanically without the light connection — functions listed, not yet reasoned.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A plant is growing in a pot of soil on a sunny windowsill. Which part of the plant actually MAKES its food — and where does the plant get what it needs to make that food? Explain how you know.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two reason targets the dominant plant misconception — that plants take their food ready-made from the soil ('roots suck up food'). A child who understands structure–function locates food-making in the leaves and casts roots as water/mineral uptake; a child with the soil-food model says the roots feed the plant.
